title: Return Of The Repressed In Germany | NOEMA
gist: Gardels argues that the rise of neo-Nazi parties in former East Germany, which now win up to 44% in regional votes, is the return of a national identity and need for belonging that post-war liberal rationalism repressed, made worse by reunification's dislocation and the 2015 refugee influx. He contends that tighter immigration is a mainstream democratic response rather than a shift to the right, and calls for secure borders, a narrower definition of asylum, skills-based selection (as in Canada) and institutions that drive integration.

themes.theme: German far-right resurgence in the East

insights.claim: Neo-Nazi parties are steadily rising in Germany, mainly in former East Germany, while the mainstream coalitions that underpinned post-war liberal democracy are breaking down.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Political fragmentation in Europe's largest economy raises policy uncertainty and coalition-formation risk.

insights.claim: Anti-immigrant sentiment in Germany that three decades ago showed up as isolated gangs firebombing immigrant homes has since been channelled into political parties that win as much as 44% of the vote in regional elections.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Shows nationalist politics has moved from fringe violence to electoral power, which can shape fiscal, EU and migration policy.
insights.quote: Today, those sentiments have been channeled into political parties that garner as high as 44% of the vote in regional elections.

insights.claim: After reunification about 15 million East Germans were left 'orphans' of a state that no longer existed, which Syberberg argued created an especially strong longing for Heimat (homeland).
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Explains why the East is the far right's regional stronghold, so the regional political divide is likely to last.
insights.quote: They have a strong sense of Heimat precisely because they have lost their homeland

insights.claim: Heiner Müller argued that once socialism collapsed, capitalism lost its enemy and therefore its 'alibi' when people failed to thrive, and right-wing extremism took over the role of capitalism's harshest critic.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Anti-establishment economic grievance is now captured by the right, which shifts the political risk facing market-friendly policy.
insights.quote: right-wing extremism has simply assumed the role of capitalism’s harshest critic

insights.claim: Müller predicted in the 1990s that the decay of the East would only be a prelude to the disintegration of the West, and the author calls this remark prescient.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Frames Western political disintegration as a long, structural trend rather than a cyclical blip.
insights.quote: The decay of the East is only a prelude to the disintegration of the West

insights.claim: Cohn-Bendit argued in the 1990s that East Germans wrongly expected unification to lift their living standards to Western levels overnight, so they faced a future of fear in which 400,000 refugees became a target for their angst.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Shows how economic disappointment combined with migration shocks drives populist backlash, a pattern that can be watched in other regions.
insights.quote: What happens when you throw 400,000 refugees into that cauldron of angst?
insights.locator: When I spoke in those days

insights.claim: The author argues that post-war Germany became an 'alias nation' that hid its identity beneath NATO and the European community, which put a rational liberal order above a national one, and that repressed identity eventually returns in uglier forms.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Suggests that the EU and Atlanticist consensus at the core of German policy is more fragile than its institutions imply.
insights.quote: A culture made to live by an alias will inevitably revert to the identity that was repressed
insights.locator: The introduction I wrote to that

insights.claim: Syberberg argued that post-war Germany repressed its cultural uniqueness and turned instead to efficiency, mathematics, business and the 'golden calf' of materialism and the strong Deutschmark, which left a deficit of belonging.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Implies that economic success alone does not buy political stability when people lack a sense of belonging.
insights.quote: We feel safe excelling at mathematics, physics, business.

insights.claim: The author argues that the disconnect seen today began in the 1990s, when European elites such as Genscher and Mitterrand ('Nationalism means war') pushed integration while grassroots nationalism was growing, and that the alienation has grown over time.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Points to a long-running gap between elites and voters that underlies political risk to European integration.
insights.quote: The disconnect that has become so manifest today was set in motion then.

insights.claim: Angela Merkel's 2015 decision to admit some 900,000 refugees from the Syrian civil war made the alienation that had been building since the 1990s worse.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: The 2015 migration shock is a key accelerant behind today's German political realignment.
insights.quote: Chancellor Angela Merkel opened wide the country’s gates to some 900,000 refugees

insights.claim: Citing Isaiah Berlin, the author says liberals should stop treating every defence of belonging as a revival of Hitler's ghost, because 'to be human means to belong'.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Signals that the centre-left may accept identity and border politics, which could change electoral strategies.
insights.quote: To be human means to belong

themes.theme: Immigration restriction as mainstream, not right-wing

insights.claim: The author argues it is wrong to describe governments that tighten immigration as 'moving to the right', because the failure to balance host populations and newcomers has become a mainstream concern that democracies are rightly responding to.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Expect stricter migration policy across the political spectrum, not only from populist parties, which matters for labour supply assumptions.
insights.quote: democratic systems are only responding as they should
insights.locator: In this context, it is wrong

insights.claim: The tension between belonging and compassion for migrants is global, affecting all of Europe, the United States and developing regions from South Africa to the Bangladesh-India borderlands.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Migration-driven political stress is a cross-market factor, not a problem specific to Germany.
insights.locator: The conundrum of how to calibrate

insights.claim: The author argues that states have a duty to control immigration using criteria that ensure newcomers follow local norms and contribute economically, because states are bound by the fiscal realities of bordered territories.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Fiscal sustainability is being used to justify selective, skills-based migration regimes.
insights.quote: states are bound by the fiscal realities of bordered territories

insights.claim: The author warns that without secure borders enforced in advance, states end up with mean-spirited and cruel crackdowns after the fact, as in the US today and on the Mediterranean, and endorses James Talarico's image of a border as a front porch with a welcome mat and a locked door.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Reactive enforcement is a sign of political overshoot; early, orderly controls may lower tail risks.
insights.quote: Our border should be like a front porch — it should have a welcome mat out front and a lock on the door

insights.claim: The author argues asylum should be redefined: it was meant for people persecuted by their governments or temporarily fleeing war, not as a route to permanent residency for mass exodus from weak states, and extending it so broadly overwhelms the cultural, political and economic carrying capacity of states.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Signals pressure to reform asylum regimes in the EU and US, which affects migration flows and labour markets.
insights.quote: Extending asylum so broadly overwhelms the carrying capacity — culturally, politically and economically — of even the most compassionate states.

insights.claim: The author says the next challenge in asylum policy will be climate refugees displaced by floods, droughts and famines tied to global warming, for which the industrialised North is historically most responsible.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Climate-driven migration is a coming source of political and fiscal pressure on rich countries.
insights.locator: The next conundrum on this front

insights.claim: The author says aging societies in the North must drop the illusion that they can do without legal immigration, which means a more multicultural mix and proactive assimilation policies.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Demographics make continued immigration necessary for labour supply; the investable question is how well integration is managed.
insights.quote: aging societies in the North must shed the illusion that they can live without legal immigration
insights.locator: Fourth, aging societies in the North

insights.claim: In Sweden, immigrants who lack the skills and education to compete for jobs are among the least integrated in Europe, and their children are disproportionately involved in violent street gangs; the Parisian suburbs show a similar pattern of immigrant silos hardening into economic castes.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Failed integration has lasting social and security costs that feed political backlash.
insights.locator: The aim must be to prevent

insights.claim: Canada integrates immigrants better than most countries because about 60% are admitted through the 'economic class', whereas Harvard's Paul May finds that two-thirds of US permanent residents are admitted for family reunification and less than 20% on skills.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Skills-based selection is presented as the model for better labour-market outcomes from immigration.
insights.quote: Canada is more successful at integrating immigrants than most because some 60% are admitted through the “economic class,”

insights.claim: Where borders are shared and demand for low-wage labour in agriculture, services and construction is high, as between the US and Mexico, the author proposes a cross-border work-permit system that does not grant permanent residency, with labour rights rigorously enforced.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A guest-worker system would affect labour costs in US agriculture, services and construction.
insights.locator: In areas where borders are contiguous

insights.claim: California's integration of a mostly second-generation Latino and Asian majority has largely worked because public higher education acts as a mixer and a transmission belt to the middle class; the California State University system has 470,000 students on 23 campuses, 48% Latino and 16% Asian.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Public higher education is shown to be key infrastructure for upward mobility and integration.
insights.quote: The California State University System has 470,000 students at 23 campuses in every region of the state.

insights.claim: The author concludes that open societies need defined borders to sustain a shared identity, that each depends on the other, and that balancing belonging with becoming is the 21st-century challenge closest to home.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Sums up the author's view that border control is a precondition for keeping liberal democracy stable.
insights.quote: Open societies need defined borders to sustain a common sense of identity.
